toc.title: Shame and being unable to move

blocks.p: I created a resource called [SSIEC](piece:snb154-ssiec-state-sensation-impulse-emotion-cognition). It stands for state, sensation, impulse, emotion, and cognition. It's how our sensations, impulses, emotions, and cognitions connect to our Polyvagal state. Some of the impulses and cognitions it lists for freeze don't make obvious sense at first, especially the impulse of release, and thoughts like grandiose or shaming. So let's walk through freeze, why it wants to release, and how it shapes our thinking.

Let's put an image to this. Imagine a spring. If you push down on a spring, you can immobilize it, but it has all this tension inside. It wants to release. Once you let go of the immobilization, it releases.

I conceptualize freeze similarly. Someone, or any mammal, goes through something and tenses up. To get out of that situation, the freeze energy is supposed to explode into aggression or evasion: fighting back or running away. It's one big release, one big burst of movement out of that frozen state.

Freeze is a combination of flight or fight plus shutdown: sympathetic plus dorsal vagal. The immobilization of shutdown compresses the flight or fight activation. So it's really the flight or fight activation that's ready to explode, and the immobilization of shutdown is what keeps it pushed in. You experience the activation and the immobilization at the same time, and that can be felt as tension. The flight or fight is there, but it's stuck. It can't be used for what it's for, running away or aggression, because it's immobilized by shutdown.

For traumatized people stuck in freeze, that activation can linger day to day, because the squeeze of immobilization is still on. It can also be triggered in a specific moment by a cue of the original event.

When freeze gets triggered, the flight or fight is triggered along with the shutdown, so it just stays compressed. What ends up happening is that it explodes into rage or panic, which is too much. That's a dysregulated release.

What we want is a regulated release. We want safety active, to turn down the shutdown. As that immobilization eases up, we want the flight or fight to expand gradually. We don't want the spring to explode.
So as more safety comes on, shutdown can come off, hopefully little by little. And as that happens, flight or fight can release a little bit at a time.

Let's ground ourselves back in what freeze is. Flight or fight is active, but it's frozen in place by dorsal vagal immobilization. You can stay with the spring, which I picture as jittery. Or imagine a car where you're slamming on the accelerator and the brake at the same time. The wheels spin, the engine gets loud and revs, the car shakes.

If that's the state of the body, what happens to our thoughts? In that highly revved state, with really no safety active, thinking matches the state of the body. And the body is in a state of danger and life threat. Here's how that shows up in the cognitions on the SSIEC sheet.

Thinking becomes very black or white. Very extreme. At the extreme, there's no safety present, so there's no empathy, no compassion, no consideration. It's just: I'm activated, but I can't do anything with it.

In that state, you can't really focus on one thing. This is probably more the panicky flavor of freeze, because freeze can be rageful, or panicky, or overwhelmed and stressed. Scattered thinking could happen in flight or fight too. But in a panicky freeze, thoughts are all over the place. You can't identify the issue or where the danger is coming from. You focus on this, and then this, and then this.

Or you can go the other way and overly focus, to the point of obsession. I consider this with OCD: as a way to contain that out-of-control flight or fight activation, the person's behavioral adaptation might be to overly focus on something in particular, or to create a ritual, like locking something six times. The ritual doesn't solve the problem, but it might contain the flight or fight activation that's spinning its wheels, and lower it enough to move on to the next step, like going to bed. That's the obsession. The compulsion is acting on it.
Flashbacks are specifically the memory: an image, or a re-experiencing, of the event that put someone into freeze.

I see grandiose thinking as a cognitive adaptation. It doesn't solve anything. But if someone in freeze can focus on how incredible they are, on being so much better, or so much more capable than they really are, that might help reduce their freeze activation. It might give a sense of containment for the activation inside. It's not a conscious thought. No one is really choosing to do this. I'd call it a cognitive adaptation, versus a behavioral one like the ritual.

Shaming probably comes from the nature of where freeze comes from. Freeze often comes from acute traumatic incidents, something a person went through, and a lot of times those are assaults of various kinds. They can leave someone feeling disgusting, shameful, ashamed. But it's really more about what was done to them. The person who did it is inflicting their shame onto another.

So depending on how you got there in the first place, the thoughts in a stuck freeze state might be "I'm a bad person" or "I did a bad thing." Shame and guilt are different. Guilt is "I did something wrong, and I feel bad about it." Shame is "There's something wrong with me, at my core, as a person."
No one is born like that. I would assume shame like that comes from repeated incidents that left someone in more of a freeze state, though it could come from one as well.

blocks.h: Shame and being unable to move

blocks.p: What if we were assaulted and couldn't move, couldn't defend ourselves, were frozen, and now we feel ashamed? Is that all linked together?

Yes, it could be. That's usually the case with the people I work with, plus the messages we get from caretakers and trusted people in our lives. Shame can come from a lot of places, but it can be connected with freeze. I think disgust can go along with shame, and so can revulsion, and both can be connected to the freeze state in particular.
Can you work with the cognitions first and have that impact the state, the sensations, and the emotions? Can you start there and make your way up?

Yes. Many times that's where we start. Learning something like the Polyvagal Theory or attachment theory, or for some people a modality like internal family systems, gives you a top-down piece of knowledge that can help you make sense of, or contain, what's happening within you.
A common top-down process I use has three steps:

ol: Validate it. Can you name what you feel?
Normalize it. Can you make sense of it?
Give it permission. Can you then give it permission to be there?

blocks.p: That's all pretty much top-down. Once you do that, the more bottom-up, felt experience can occur. So working with the cognitions can be a way to calm, to contain, to make sense of, and even eventually to allow what's happening from the bottom up.
